Rain & elevation

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows why a low elevation angle gives a longer path through the same rain layer.

A supplied empirical model gives specific attenuation γR = kRᵅ in dB/km for rain rate R in mm/h. Its coefficients depend on the adopted propagation model and conditions.

For a flat uniform rain layer of vertical thickness hR − hs, the path length is L = (hR − hs)/sin E. Total attenuation is γRL, with consistent distance units.

This geometric approximation lengthens the path as elevation falls. Earth's curvature, limited rain-cell size, and nonuniform weather become important near the horizon, so a flat-layer extrapolation needs a defined range of validity.

Example

A 4 km vertical rain thickness with γR = 2 dB/km gives 8 dB attenuation at zenith and 16 dB at 30° elevation in this uniform-layer model.

    1. For the same uniform rain layer, how does attenuation change from 90° to 30° elevation?

    Compare 1/sin 90° with 1/sin 30°.

    The modeled rain path and attenuation both double. This comparison keeps specific attenuation and layer thickness fixed.
